records.title: Transit spectroscopy and atmospheric inference
records.source_org: NASA Science / NASA Exoplanet Exploration Program
records.core_fact: Transit spectroscopy analyzes starlight that has traveled through an exoplanet atmosphere; spectral patterns can support inference about atmospheric molecules.
what_it_does_not_prove: A spectrum alone proves life, intelligence, or technology.
Every molecule identification is unambiguous or independent of model/instrument assumptions.
The telescope directly photographed the molecule or planet surface.
The same inference applies to every planet or observing setup.
records.source_locator: NASA page section “Transit Spectroscopy: Reading the Light”; evidence package locator lines 309–316.
records.freshness_policy: Recheck NASA methodology page within 24 months; recheck named detections/examples at use time.
records.notes: Normalized from RAC-001 evidence. Scope intentionally narrowed from broad remote observation to transit spectroscopy. Source artifact hash was not obtained in the research environment. records.title: Habitable zone does not mean inhabited
records.core_fact: A habitable-zone classification describes orbital conditions under which surface liquid water may be possible in a defined model; it does not confirm that a world has life.
what_it_does_not_prove: Life exists on a planet in the zone.
A planet is actually habitable without relevant atmospheric, geological, and other evidence.
A planet is safe or suitable for people.
A planet outside a simplified zone cannot support any life under any conditions.
records.source_locator: NASA Science ‘Fast facts: What is the Habitable Zone?’; supporting caution also recorded from NASA Astrobiology’s Kepler-186f article.
records.freshness_policy: Recheck NASA definition within 24 months; any named planet/example must be checked at use time.
records.notes: Secondary evidence URL and historical-example context remain in RAC-002.md. Source artifact hash was not obtained. records.title: Europa subsurface-ocean inference
records.topic: Evidence for an inferred ocean beneath Europa’s ice
records.core_fact: Multiple independent observations, including Galileo magnetic measurements, strongly support the inference that Europa has a global salty ocean beneath its ice.
what_it_does_not_prove: Life exists in Europa’s ocean.
The ocean’s exact depth, salinity, chemistry, or habitability is already established.
A suspected plume is a confirmed ocean sample.
Current or future mission objectives are already completed results.
records.source_locator: NASA ‘Evidence for an Ocean’ sections ‘Why We Think Europa Has an Ocean’ and ‘Galileo’.
records.freshness_policy: Stable evidence claim: review within 24 months. Mission status/objectives are excluded from core_fact and must be checked separately when mentioned.
records.notes: B2 review required splitting stable ocean inference from time-sensitive Europa Clipper mission status; this normalized record does so. Source artifact hash was not obtained. records.title: Planetary protection and contamination control
records.topic: NASA planetary-protection requirements for covered missions
records.source_org: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance
records.core_fact: NASA planetary-protection policy limits biological or relevant molecular contamination for covered robotic missions, with requirements depending on target and mission type.
what_it_does_not_prove: Every space mission is subject to identical procedures.
Every mission component is sterile.
NASA robotic-mission rules apply unchanged to all private, crewed, or foreign missions.
A policy category is evidence of life at a target.
records.source_locator: NPR 8715.24 Chapter 1 §§1.1.1–1.2.1; related NASA-STD-8719.27 and handbook references are recorded in RAC-004.md.
records.freshness_policy: Policy asset: recheck at least every 6 months and on NASA/COSPAR/Outer Space Treaty policy changes.
records.notes: Scope remains explicitly NASA/covered missions; it must not be generalized into universal international law. Source artifact hash was not obtained. records.title: How IPCC AR6 communicates confidence and likelihood
records.core_fact: IPCC AR6 Working Group I assesses confidence using evidence and agreement, and uses calibrated likelihood language when there is a sufficient probabilistic basis.
what_it_does_not_prove: IPCC’s calibrated categories apply to all scientific institutions or all research papers.
Low confidence means a claim is false or all alternatives have equal support.
A model output is an observation or any model result is reliable without validation.
A probability can be assigned without evidence or a defined outcome.
records.source_locator: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 1, Box 1.1 ‘Treatment of Uncertainty and Calibrated Uncertainty Language in AR6’.
records.freshness_policy: Review on a new IPCC assessment/method note; otherwise within 24 months.
records.notes: Deliberately institution-scoped; not a universal rule for all science. Tier A is based on formal scientific-assessment-source status. records.title: Generative-AI confabulation risk
records.source_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
records.core_fact: NIST identifies confidently presented false or erroneous generated content (‘confabulation’) as a risk for generative AI.
what_it_does_not_prove: Every AI answer is false or unreliable.
A named model or current product has a particular error rate.
All generative systems behave identically.
NIST requires every user to use the same verification workflow.
External evidence checks guarantee correctness.
records.source_locator: NIST AI 600-1, §2 risk 2 ‘Confabulation’, pp. 12–13; publication record also cited in RAC-007.md.
records.freshness_policy: Review at least every 12 months and whenever NIST AI 600-1/profile is revised; product-specific claims require separate versioned evidence.
records.notes: One of the strongest first-shelf AI assets. The source supports the risk definition, not a universal user-side verification ritual. records.title: UNESCO MIL guidance on evaluating information and providers
records.topic: Information/source evaluation in UNESCO media and information literacy
records.core_fact: UNESCO’s Media and Information Literacy curriculum includes evaluating information, content, and providers, and notes that educational and media content can be biased, incomplete, or erroneous.
what_it_does_not_prove: A source from a named category is always true or unbiased.
Comparing two sources always resolves a disputed claim.
Every learner using the curriculum will improve measured media literacy.
UNESCO specifies one universal ranking of sources independent of the information need.
records.source_locator: UNESCO MIL Curriculum Part 1, pp. 25–27, section ‘Evaluation of Information, Media and Digital Communications’.
records.freshness_policy: Recheck on UNESCO edition update; otherwise within 24 months.
records.notes: This record is a fact about UNESCO’s published curriculum/guidance, not an efficacy study. Generalized normative reuse must retain the named-source guidance context. records.title: W3C WAI guidance on image alternatives
records.topic: Context-sensitive image alternatives in web accessibility guidance
records.source_org: World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), Web Accessibility Initiative
records.core_fact: W3C WAI guidance says image alternatives should reflect an image’s relevant information or function in context, and complex informative images may require a fuller equivalent.
what_it_does_not_prove: A particular visual design is universally easier to perceive.
Image size, contrast, or style has one effect for all viewers and contexts.
All meaningful visual evidence must be narrated or text can replace every visual experience.
The WAI tutorial validates a specific Galaxy visual design.
records.source_locator: W3C WAI Images Tutorial sections on informative, decorative, functional and complex images; related informative-images page cited in RAC-009.md.
records.freshness_policy: Check on W3C/WCAG revision; otherwise within 24 months. Use exact WCAG edition if claiming compliance.
records.notes: This record is about W3C accessibility guidance, not a universal empirical law about child perception or visual preference. records.title: Digital.gov usability testing with prototypes
records.topic: Observing intended users performing tasks with products/prototypes
records.core_fact: Digital.gov’s usability guide describes observing intended users as they attempt realistic tasks with a product or prototype as one way to identify design issues and user needs.
what_it_does_not_prove: Testing guarantees a design will meet every user’s needs.
The guide’s method is the only valid design or research method.
A test with one user or one task is sufficient for all purposes.
Observed behavior automatically explains why the behavior occurred.
records.source_locator: Digital.gov ‘Usability testing’ guide, sections ‘What’, ‘Why’, and steps 1–7; step 1 permits a sketch or prototype.
records.freshness_policy: Source page has no displayed revision date; review on page change and at least every 12 months.
records.notes: This is a source-scoped public-sector practice-guide proposition, not causal proof that one test guarantees usability.
